title: Bailey Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Bailey wells have a 300 ft median depth and 5.0 gpm median yield. Review local drilling costs, water levels and checks before buying mountain property.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Bailey
intro_html:
A Bailey well is a fractured-rock project, not a predictable tap into a uniform underground reservoir. Local records show a 300 ft median depth, but the middle half runs from 180-480 ft. That spread matters when pricing a lot or comparing drilling bids.

This page covers Colorado DWR permit records within 5 miles of Bailey in Park County: 6,784 permits, with 4,883 wells recorded as constructed. Use these figures as a local starting point, then narrow your research to the wells closest to the property.

sections.heading: Why Bailey Drilling Bids Need Room for Depth
sections.html:
Across 5,021 wells reporting depth, Bailey's median is 300 ft. The middle half falls between 180-480 ft, and the 90th percentile reaches 680 ft. A bid based only on the median leaves a meaningful risk of additional footage.

The ground here is fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. Water comes through fractures rather than a continuous, evenly productive layer. Permits overwhelmingly identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers; Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 0% of this dataset.

Nearby Pine and Conifer provide useful regional context, but the closest well logs are better bidding references. Ask the driller how additional footage, casing and grout are charged if usable fractures are deeper than expected.

sections.heading: A Bailey Well's Yield Matters as Much as Its Depth
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 5.0 gpm, with the middle half between 2.0-7.0 gpm. Those figures come from 2,768 wells reporting yield, not every permit in the area. They describe recorded performance, not a guarantee of what a well will deliver today.

For a buyer, the important caution is that 9% report less than 1 gpm. A low-producing well may need storage and careful demand management, and deeper drilling does not automatically solve the problem.

Have an existing well tested for sustained production and recovery. Household demand arrives in bursts, so review the pump, storage and well performance together rather than treating a reported yield as a complete water-supply assessment.

sections.heading: Bailey Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to standing water when the well is not pumping. It is not the drilled depth. Among 302 reporting wells around Bailey, the median is 80 ft below ground, with a middle half of 42-200 ft.

Decade medians move from 54 ft in the 1970s to 40 ft in the 1980s, 64 ft in the 1990s, 52 ft in the 2000s, 132 ft in the 2010s and 80 ft in the 2020s. That is not a steady downward trend.

These measurements also are not repeated readings from the same wells. They cannot establish property-specific decline. For a purchase, current static and pumping levels, recovery testing and any older measurements from that well are more useful.

sections.heading: Bailey's Well Records Reflect Decades of Mountain Building
sections.html:
The largest permit decade in the Bailey records was the 1990s, with 1,873 permits, followed by the 1970s with 1,646. Records include 338 permits from the 2010s and 196 from the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The current decade is incomplete, and permit totals should not be treated as completed-well totals.

The most active drillers listed are Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert), with 1,025 records; Stan'S Drilling (Stansbury, Larry), with 690; and Ernie'S Mountain Drilling Inc. (Malovich, Ernest J), with 388. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability.

Domestic/household use represents 94% of permits. Still, check the actual permit: a household-use authorization does not automatically allow outdoor watering or livestock.

sections.heading: Budgeting a Finished Well on a Bailey Lot
sections.html:
For Bailey's fractured granite and gneiss, the supplied drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 300 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $19,500-$30,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $25,500-$42,000.

Those are planning figures, not a parcel-specific quote. The local 180-480 ft middle-half depth range is a reason to compare footage assumptions before comparing bottom-line prices.

Request a written scope showing casing, grout, testing, pump equipment and utility connections. On a mountain lot, rig access and the route from the well to the house also deserve an on-site review. Keep driveway, septic and broader site-development work clearly separated from the well estimate.

sections.heading: Check Bailey Water Quality and Low-Yield Risk Separately
sections.html:
Environmental mapping within about 10 miles identifies 1 PFAS sampling/contamination site, 17 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. These are screening flags, not evidence that a particular Bailey well is contaminated. Their mapped radius is also broader than the well-statistics area.

Before closing, obtain laboratory water testing and use nearby site information to decide whether additional testing is appropriate. Review casing condition, the well cap, surface drainage and the relationship between the well and septic system.

Water quality and water quantity are separate questions. The 9% share reporting under 1 gpm makes production testing important even when water tests clean. Fractured rock also carries dry-hole risk; ask how unsuccessful drilling would be handled before work starts.

sections.heading: Before You Buy or Build Near Bailey
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit and available construction records. Confirm that the well serves the property being sold and that its permitted uses match your plans. An existing permit is not proof of a working water supply, and a new lot needs permit feasibility checked before you commit to construction.

Compare neighboring depths and yields, but do not assume a successful well in Pine or Brook Forest predicts the result on your lot. Local fractures can change over short distances.

Have the driller and site contractor review rig access, the house location, septic layout and utility routes together. For an existing home, make satisfactory production testing, water-quality results and permit review part of the purchase decision rather than work left until after closing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Bailey, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Bailey, the median recorded well depth is 300 ft. The middle half runs from 180-480 ft, and the 90th percentile is 680 ft. Fractured granite and gneiss make depth variable, so use nearby construction logs and a bid with clear additional-footage pricing rather than assuming your well will reach water at the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Bailey?
faq.a: The Bailey cost model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 300 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $19,500-$30,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $25,500-$42,000. Actual pricing depends on depth, construction requirements, access and the connection route to the house.

faq.q: How much water does a well in Bailey produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields around Bailey have a 5.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 2.0-7.0 gpm. However, 9% report less than 1 gpm. Before buying, arrange a production and recovery test. A historic yield entry does not establish current performance, and low-yield wells may require storage and careful management of household demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Bailey, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records cannot establish whether a particular Bailey well is safe to drink. Mapping within about 10 miles identifies 1 PFAS sampling/contamination site, 17 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, but proximity alone does not prove contamination. Get laboratory testing and review nearby environmental records, well construction and septic conditions before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Bailey?
faq.a: The available records do not show a steady decline. Median static water depth was 52 ft in the 2000s, 132 ft in the 2010s and 80 ft in the 2020s. Only 302 wells report static levels, and decade summaries do not track the same wells over time. Evaluate the property's own measurement history and current pumping performance.
